nameStory: The fingernailclam gets its name from its tiny size and translucent, curved shell that looks remarkably like a human fingernail clipping. The "Herrington" part honors malacologist Harry Herrington, who studied freshwater mollusks in the early 1900s. These little clams are so small they often go unnoticed despite being quite common in New England waters.
description: The Herrington fingernailclam is a tiny freshwater bivalve mollusk that measures only about 6-10 millimeters across - roughly the size of a small button. Its shell is nearly round with a subtle point at one end, colored pale yellow to light brown with a glossy, almost translucent appearance. Like other fingernailclams, it's a filter feeder that lives buried in muddy or sandy lake and pond bottoms. Despite its small size, it plays an important role in filtering water and providing food for fish and waterfowl.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Nearly circular shell with subtle triangular outline when viewed from above, feeling smooth and slightly slippery when wet

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 6-10mm across, about the size of your pinky fingernail or a small shirt button

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale yellow to light brown, often with a translucent quality that lets you see through the thin shell

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: Shell feels glassy smooth with very faint growth lines that you can barely feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Hinge area
idTips.description: Small, pointed beak (umbo) positioned slightly toward one end rather than dead center

habitat: Found in shallow areas of lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, particularly in muddy or sandy bottoms rich in organic matter. They prefer areas with some aquatic vegetation and are often discovered along shorelines where gentle wave action has washed them up. Look for them in water 1-6 feet deep, often associated with cattails, pondweeds, and other emergent plants.

seasonality.spring: Active and reproducing as waters warm; shells may wash up on shorelines after spring storms and ice-out.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're actively filtering and growing; easiest time to find live specimens in shallow water.
seasonality.fall: Still active but preparing for winter dormancy; empty shells often accumulate on beaches after fall storms.
seasonality.winter: Dormant in bottom sediments under ice; only empty shells visible on shorelines until spring thaw.

funFact: Herrington fingernailclams are hermaphrodites that brood their babies in special gill pouches, releasing tiny fully-formed clams instead of helpless larvae - imagine giving birth to teenagers instead of babies!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other fingernailclams in the same genus, but the Herrington's more circular outline and slightly off-center hinge point help distinguish it. Remember: "Herrington's round, others are ground" - meaning this species is more circular while relatives tend to be more oval or rhomboid-shaped.
contextualKnowledge: The term "fingernailclam" sometimes causes confusion with marine clams, but these are strictly freshwater mollusks. They're also called "pea clams" due to their small size, though they're actually smaller than most peas.
compareHints: Herrington fingernailclam is more circular than its relatives - the Grooved fingernailclam has distinct ridges you can feel, the Rhomboid is diamond-shaped, and the Striated has obvious parallel lines across the shell. If the shell feels perfectly smooth and looks nearly round, you've likely found a Herrington.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its fingernailclam relatives, the grooved species stands out for its pronounced concentric ridges, while the rhomboid fingernailclam is more diamond-shaped and the striated species has finer, more closely-spaced lines.

The rhomboid fingernailclam's diamond-shaped outline distinguishes it from its relatives: the grooved fingernailclam has prominent concentric ridges and a more oval shape, while the striated fingernailclam shows distinct radiating lines from the shell's peak.
The Striated Fingernailclam differs from the Grooved Fingernailclam by having finer, more numerous ridges across its shell surface.
